w: An 1875 uprising burned this building nearly to the ground, and the nickname Quemado -- Burnt Palace -- stuck through every rebuild since. It housed Bolivia's presidents from 1853 until Evo Morales moved to the Casa Grande del Pueblo in 2018, briefly returning under Jeanine Anez in 2019-2020. It now operates as a museum.

w: Aymara yatiri healers run this market along Linares, Jimenez, Santa Cruz and Illampu streets, selling dried frogs, medicinal herbs and love potions alongside fortune-telling and curses. Its best-known item is the sullu, a dried llama fetus buried under house foundations as an offering to Pachamama.

w: Franciscans raised this church between 1743 and 1772 under the invocation of Francis of Assisi, adding its tower only at the close of the nineteenth century. w: The first La Paz cathedral took 70 years to build and was demolished by 1831 after its presbytery began collapsing. This replacement, begun in 1835, wasn't inaugurated until 1925. Neoclassical with Baroque touches, its five naves hold a chapel for Marshal Andres de Santa Cruz; its twin towers opened only in 1989.

w: Opened in 1984 on Jaen Street in La Paz's old town, this museum occupies a historic building that carries Bolivia's monumental heritage status in its own right. Its collection is devoted entirely to pre-Columbian precious metalwork -- gold and silver objects worked long before Spanish colonisation reached the Andes.

Jutting from the hills south of the city, its jagged silhouette has become one of the most recognisable landmarks on the La Paz skyline.
